items.title: Albert Nicholas Interview, 1972-06-26
items.q: Bonnie was playing some beautiful clarinet with Duke.

ctx.x: To get back to the early days, did you watch the other clarinet players carefully? Did you watch them to figure out anything?

Yes, you sure you got ears. I tell you, when I was coming up, I admired Artie Shaw was my favorite clarinet player. Benny Goodman, he played nice, but he was a mechanical to me. I didn't copy him, but I knew what they were making. But Artie Shaw had something else. He had a beautiful sound. He was a great musician. And this man was something else. I liked his band, Artie Shaw, in the third. You had another one you had. You had a lot of clarinet players. But it was all imitating Benny. And that was a little, Benny…
up saxophone yourself were there any others before you no i'll tell you what i would take

items.title: Albert Nicholas Interview, 1967-02-09
items.q: I've seen him ask Duke, come on and sit down and play a little bit. And Duke wouldn't follow that.

ctx.x: That's right. Well, not the sort of swing you know. Why do you think that Jelly didn't have very much influence on musicians that came after him? Whereas other pianists, like Earl Hines, had tremendous influence on them?

Well, Jelly was a different person from Earl Hines, you see. As I told you, his thinking was different. Jelly was a great musician, but he wasn't commercialized. Jelly had two or three bands, you know what I mean? Coming up in the early 30s. And he just didn't care about going through all these headaches, to build a band, to continue on. He figured his name was there. He was Jelly Roll Morton. He was different. He was just a different, he was a character, as I said. Money didn't mean nothing to Jelly. He was a…
Duke was being quoted as saying that he thought Jelly was a very bad musician.
